html:
The release of two dozen wild European rabbits for hunting by the settler Thomas Austin on his property near Geelong, Victoria, in October 1859. Within decades they had spread across much of the continent.

Rabbits had come with the First Fleet in 1788, but those were tame animals kept in hutches. Austin's wild rabbits, and their crosses with tame ones, found a land with few predators, mild winters and pasture cleared for sheep. They spread faster than any other mammal known to have colonised a new land, reaching hundreds of millions. They stripped grass, killed young trees, pushed native animals out and competed with sheep for feed, helping turn droughts into disasters.

Settlers tried shooting, trapping, poison and fences. Western Australia built the Rabbit-proof Fence in the early 1900s. In 1950 the government released the myxoma virus, which killed most rabbits until they grew resistant, and in the 1990s a second virus. Rabbits are still a major pest. Compare the cane toads brought in later to fight beetles.
